content: The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines are developed with the primary goal of serving the health and well-being of populations globally or within specific regions or countries. These guidelines are created to provide recommendations that improve public health outcomes. To ensure the integrity of this process, WHO follows a rigorous methodology to avoid or effectively manage conflicts of interest. Conflicts of interest arise when secondary interests—such as personal, financial, or professional motivations—interfere with the primary objective of improving public health. While secondary interests, such as a researcher’s desire to publish findings or a stakeholder’s advocacy for a specific condition, are often legitimate, they can become problematic if they conflict with the primary goal. This misalignment may lead to decisions that undermine the primary interest of public health. To enhance transparency and public trust, WHO discloses the names and brief biographies of individuals being considered for participation in its Guideline Development Groups. This information is made available for public notice and comment. The experts themselves provide the disclosed information, and WHO is not responsible for its accuracy or completeness. Comments received through this process are treated confidentially and are acknowledged via a generic email notification. These comments are integral to WHO’s conflict of interest assessment and are carefully reviewed. WHO reserves the right to discuss the information received with the relevant expert and may disclose the name and affiliation of the individual providing the information. Based on its review, WHO may take appropriate management actions in line with its policies. Participation in a WHO-convened Guideline Development Group does not imply that the views expressed by the expert represent WHO’s official policies or decisions. The list of participating experts, their disclosed relevant interests, and any mitigation measures taken by WHO to manage conflicts of interest are reported publicly in accordance with WHO policies. Expert Biographies: 1. Lisa Bero Lisa Bero is a Professor and Chair of Medicines Use and Health Outcomes at the University of Sydney’s School of Pharmacy and Charles Perkins Centre. She is an internationally recognized researcher in evidence-based healthcare, focusing on the integrity of clinical and basic research evidence used to influence health policy. She leads the Evidence, Policy, and Influence Collaborative, which explores evidence synthesis, bias reduction, and pharmaceutical policy. She is also a Senior Editor for Cochrane Public Health and Health Systems Network and has served on committees addressing conflicts of interest and evidence-based decision-making. 2. Yingyao Chen Yingyao Chen is a Professor of Health Services at Fudan University’s School of Public Health and serves as the Director of the Key Lab of Health Technology Assessment and the WHO Collaborating Center for Health Technology Assessment and Management. His expertise includes health technology assessment, health policy, health economics, and hospital management. He holds leadership roles in public health economics and birth defects prevention committees in China. 3. Amadou Moctar Dièye Amadou Moctar Dièye is the Director of Laboratories at Senegal’s Ministry of Health and a Professor of Pharmacology at Université Cheikh Anta Diop de Dakar. His expertise includes promoting the use of generic medicines, clinical trials, pharmacovigilance, and anti-doping policies. He has also analyzed marketing authorization applications for human and veterinary medicines. 4. Andrew Hill Andrew Hill is a Senior Visiting Research Fellow at the University of Liverpool, specializing in treatment access issues. His research focuses on the production costs of drugs for HIV, viral hepatitis, tuberculosis, and cancer. He has worked with organizations such as WHO, UNITAID, and the Clinton Foundation. He holds a PhD from the University of Amsterdam and has a background in HIV research from Oxford University and St. Mary’s Hospital in London. 5. Tanya Potashnik Tanya Potashnik is the Director of Policy and Economic Analysis at Canada’s Patented Medicines Prices Review Board. With over 25 years of experience in pharmaceutical pricing, regulation, and reimbursement, she has played a pivotal role in advancing health technology assessment (HTA) in Canada and implementing regulatory changes to lower drug costs. Her work focuses on improving access and affordability for patients while ensuring the sustainability of Canada’s publicly funded healthcare system. 6. Shadi Saleh Shadi Saleh is the Founding Director of the Global Health Institute and a Professor of Health System and Financing at the American University of Beirut. His expertise includes evidence-based decision-making, economic evaluation, and healthcare financing policy. He has contributed to innovative solutions in the pharmaceutical industry and serves as an advisor to the World Bank, WHO, and UN on healthcare financing and system strengthening projects. 7. Vania Cristina Canuto Santos Vania Cristina Canuto Santos is a health economist and Director at Brazil’s National Commission for Health Technologies Incorporation (CONITEC). She has extensive experience in pharmaceutical price regulation and has worked on health technology assessment and policy development within Brazil’s public health system. 8. Sakthivel Selvaraj Sakthivel Selvaraj is the Director and Professor of Health Economics, Financing, and Policy at the Public Health Foundation of India. His work focuses on healthcare financing, access to medicines, and pharmaceutical policy. He has contributed to the development of India’s Universal Health Coverage (UHC) policies and state health policies, as well as research on pharmaceutical financing and supply chain management. 9. Netnapis Suchonwanich Netnapis Suchonwanich is an advisor to Thailand’s Health Intervention and Technology Assessment Program (HITAP). She has played a key role in the development of Thailand’s Universal Health Coverage (UHC) scheme and health insurance information systems. She has also served on committees for essential medicines and price negotiation in Thailand. 10. Fatima Suleman Fatima Suleman is a Professor at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa and Chair of the Pricing Committee for Medicines for South Africa’s Ministry of Health. Her research focuses on pharmaceutical policy and systems. She has served on WHO panels and contributed to the development of affordable therapeutics for public health. 11. Sabine Vogler Sabine Vogler is the Director of the WHO Collaborating Centre for Pharmaceutical Pricing and Reimbursement Policies and Head of the Pharmacoeconomics Department at the Austrian Public Health Institute. She has extensive expertise in pharmaceutical pricing, reimbursement, and cost-containment reforms. She has coordinated several research projects at national and European levels and serves on editorial boards for journals related to pharmacoeconomics and health systems research.
